notes.1a: A significant minority of candidates appeared to have little experience of using a burette and could not read the volumes. The commonest error was recording volumes as whole numbers such as 3 3 8 cm or 0 cm . Candidates should realise that burettes measure volumes to (at least) one decimal 3 3 place. Therefore, the expected readings would be 8.0 cm or 0.0 cm .
notes.1b: The colour change for methyl orange was well known.
notes.1c: Only about half of the candidates observed bubbles or fizzing.
notes.1di: This was generally correctly answered. Most candidates realised that a larger volume of acid was used in Experiment 1, but fewer went on to give a quantitative answer, such as it was twice as much.
notes.1dii: Most could explain the difference in volumes was because of the different concentrations of the acids. Vague reference to different solutions or strengths of acids were common.
notes.1e: Most candidates could not deduce the volume of solution L needed.
notes.1f: This was well answered. Most knew that the burette was rinsed to remove contaminants from the previous experiment.
notes.1g: Vague answers referred to drying the burette. Few understood that the burette should then be rinsed with solution L to remove the remaining water, which would otherwise dilute solution L when placed in the burette.
notes.1h: The use of a white tile to make the colour change of the indicator more obvious gained credit. A range of incorrect answers referred to ‘stopping heat losses’, ‘improving the stability of the flask’.
notes.1hi: Repeating the experiments alone does not improve the reliability of the results. If the results are compared and found to be similar, or if anomalies are discarded, then the results are more reliable.
notes.1j: The use of a measuring cylinder was known to cause inaccuracies and most went on to replace it with a pipette or burette. Vague references to reading errors were common.
notes.2a: Candidates found it difficult to describe the sublimation of the ammonium bromide. Many candidates observed smoke, gas, or fumes, but few detailed that it was white smoke. Similarly, many reported condensation on the sides of the boiling tube but did not describe it as a white solid.
notes.2b: Most realised that there was no reaction with aqueous sodium hydroxide.
notes.2c: The majority of candidates identified ammonia and tested for it correctly.
notes.2d: Many candidates reported the formation of a cream precipitate. A significant number stated that the precipitate would be white, cream-yellow, or white cream and gained no credit.
notes.2e: Only a minority of candidates described that the solution went yellow or orange as bromine was displaced. Effervescence and formation of precipitates were common guesses.
notes.2f: Many candidates correctly identified the presence of one of the ions in solid O , with some identifying ammonium bromide. Liquid P was cyclohexene.
notes.2g: Fresh bromine water was decolourised as expected.
notes.2h: Most candidates observed a flame or the liquid burning.
notes.2hi: Expected colour changes were purple to green and then brown. Many candidates gained full credit.
notes.2j: The most common answer seen was that ‘ P was flammable’. A number of candidates recognised that P was an alkene or an unsaturated hydrocarbon.
